title: A meta-analysis of functional neuroimaging studies of ketamine administration in healthy volunteers

claims.statement: In healthy volunteers scanned while ketamine was being infused, brain activity measured as glucose use, blood flow or the fMRI signal goes up rather than down, and most at the front. In 10 volunteers given racemic ketamine, whole-brain glucose metabolism rose 24.5% (SD 14.3) from each person's own drug-free scan and rose in every participant (p<0.01); the rise was largest in the anterior cingulate (34%) and frontal cortex (30 to 34%) and smallest in the occipitomedial cortex (16 to 17%), with no decrease in any region examined, and front-to-back ratios shifted accordingly (Vollenweider et al., 1997b). In a second group of 10 given the (S)-form, regional increases ran from 19.6% in the frontomedial to 27.35% in the parietal cortex, with cortical regions about 2 to 3 times more affected than deeper structures and the whole-brain change (12%) not reaching significance (Vollenweider et al., 1997a). A 2024 meta-analysis that pooled the published peak coordinates of 33 functional-imaging studies in 628 healthy volunteers, and whose confidence the editors rate critically low, found only two clusters that survived correction for multiple testing: more activity at rest in the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (658 voxels, 495 after correction) and, during executive-function tasks, in the right Heschl's gyrus (160 voxels, 142 after correction); across all 23 task studies together nothing was significant and no decrease was found in any analysis (Ait Bentaleb et al., 2024). What these scans cannot show is which change produces which experience: both 1997 studies report every symptom-to-brain correlation as a significance level with a direction and print no correlation coefficient anywhere, they made about 150 to 180 comparisons without correcting for their number and call the analysis exploratory, one of them had no dummy condition and in the other every participant recognised the drug. All of this describes a single session with ketamine in the body, not any lasting change.
claims.magnitude: Vollenweider et al. (1997b), racemic, n=10: whole-brain glucose metabolism +24.5% (SD 14.3, Wilcoxon p<0.01, higher in every participant); cingulate anterior +34%, frontal +30 to 34%, insula +19 to 23%, parietal +18 to 25%, somatosensory +19 to 25%, motor +15 to 18%, temporal +16 to 19%, occipitomedial +16 to 17%; no decreases. Frontomedial/temporomedial ratio 1.31→1.44 (left) and 1.41→1.53 (right), frontomedial/occipitomedial 1.04→1.14 and 1.06→1.16 (all p<0.05). Vollenweider et al. (1997a), (S)-ketamine, n=10: frontomedial +19.6%, frontolateral +20.1%, cingulate anterior +23.5%, cingulate posterior +24.0%, parietal +27.35%; thalamus +17% (p<0.07); whole brain +12% (p<0.09, not significant). Ait Bentaleb et al. (2024): resting state, left anterior cingulate/paracingulate BA 24 (MNI 0; 30; 20), Z=4.265, p<0.001, 658 voxels, 495 after correction; uncorrected only, right insula BA 47 (36; 24; −6), Z=3.432, 30 voxels, and right fusiform gyrus BA 30 (22; −34; −16), Z=2.933, 26 voxels. Executive-function tasks (9 studies): right Heschl's gyrus BA 48 (44; −16; 6), Z=3.306, 160 voxels, 142 after correction; uncorrected right rostral anterior cingulate BA 10 (6; 52; 8), Z=2.889, 26 voxels. No effect size or interval is recoverable from a coordinate-based meta-analysis.
